tip: 'thuis' means at home and needs no preposition; for going home you'd use 'naar huis': Meestal eet ik thuis.
Dutch fuses time words into one: 'morgenochtend' = morgen + ochtend, tomorrow morning.
'Wellicht' means perhaps and is more formal than the everyday 'misschien'.
'beste' is the superlative of 'goed' (goed, beter, best): mijn beste vriend, my best friend.
Separable 'langskomen' (drop by) splits in the present: the prefix 'langs' moves to the end, komt hij langs.
'Daarom' means that is why, or therefore; it points back to a reason to state its result.
'fietsen' takes 'zijn', not 'hebben', in the perfect once a destination is named: is naar de winkel gefietst.
Verbs of change of state take 'zijn' in the perfect: de temperatuur is gestegen, rose.
Units of measure stay singular after a number: tien kilometer, never 'kilometers'.
'Over' plus a time span means 'in' that much time: over een uur = in an hour.
'Enkel' here means only, like 'alleen'; it is common in Belgian Dutch: enkel op dinsdag.
'Volgens mij' means in my opinion, literally 'according to me'; use 'volgens' plus a person.
'Hierna' means after this, something coming up; compare 'daarna', after that.
Dutch shows possession with 'van', not apostrophe-s: de fiets van mijn broer, my brother's bike.
You give something to someone with 'aan': ik geef de sleutel aan mijn buurman.
'hun' is the indirect-object pronoun, to them: de juf leest hun een verhaaltje voor.
'bedanken' takes 'voor' for the thing you thank someone for: bedankt haar voor de maaltijd.
'wegens' means because of, or due to, and takes a noun: geannuleerd wegens een storing.
Dutch uses 'op' for being at a workplace: op kantoor zijn, to be at the office.
Means of transport uses 'met': met de trein, by train; met de bus, met de fiets.
In the perfect a separable verb wraps 'ge-' inside: meenemen becomes meegenomen (mee + ge + nomen).
'elke' means every and is followed by a singular noun: elke dag, every day.
'zodra' (as soon as) sends its verb to the end of the clause: zodra we het weten.
Separable 'uittrekken' (take off) splits: ik trek mijn schoenen uit.
An infinitive works as a noun after 'het': na het eten = after eating, literally after the eating.
For time you use 'doorbrengen', to spend; keep 'uitgeven' for spending money: tijd doorbrengen.
'om ... te' plus an infinitive expresses purpose, in order to: om de zonsopgang te zien.
Separable 'meenemen' splits in the present: neemt altijd een paraplu mee, takes an umbrella along.
The perfect of separable 'doorlezen' keeps 'ge-' inside: doorgelezen, read through.
Clock times take 'om': om zes uur = at six o'clock.
'Doorgaans' means usually, or generally; it is a more formal version of 'meestal'.
'Inderdaad' means indeed and confirms something just said: inderdaad is het een mooi boek.
Place 'niet' before the verbs it negates: hij kan morgen niet komen werken.
'per' names a means or rate: per post, by mail; per uur, per hour.
'verdwijnen' (disappear) takes 'zijn' in the perfect: de zon is verdwenen.
'bestaan uit' means to consist of; the fixed preposition is 'uit': bestaat uit brood en kaas.
'keer' counts occurrences: drie keer, three times; twee keer, twice.
Separable 'binnensluipen' wraps 'ge-' in the perfect: binnengeslopen, sneaked in.
'Bovendien' means moreover, or besides, adding a further point to what came before.
Dutch has no verb for 'to like doing'; 'graag' plus a verb carries it: verwelkomen u graag.
'hen' is the object pronoun after a verb or preposition, them: wij kennen hen.
'zich' is the reflexive pronoun; 'zich ziek melden' means to call in sick: zij meldt zich ziek.
'een steentje bijdragen' is a fixed phrase meaning to do your bit, to contribute your part.
'heen en weer' is a set phrase meaning back and forth: de boot vaart heen en weer.
Separable 'ophangen' splits: zij hangt haar jas op, she hangs up her coat.
